pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Animal Nutrition

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Animals, including humans'):** "identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE):** No US elementary PE names food groups; the closest idea, that animals get materials and energy from food, sits within 5-PS3-1 / LS1.C ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS3-1]... and the energy'). Treat as UK-led.

- **Operational details:** The organising contrast is heterotroph vs autotroph in child terms: plants MAKE their own food (using light); animals CANNOT and must EAT it. From there children learn that food provides different things the body needs — the main food groups (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water) — and that the body needs the RIGHT TYPES and the RIGHT AMOUNTS (not just 'more is better'). Consequences of imbalance make it concrete (too little calcium → weak bones; too little of a vitamin → illness). Keep it at the level of grouping foods and matching each group to what it does; detailed nutrient chemistry is KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A Y3 child can name the food groups, sort foods into them, and state that animals must eat while plants make their own food; the conceptual stretch is 'right types AND amounts' — that a balanced variety, not a single favourite food, keeps the body healthy.
bestPractices: Lead with the plant-vs-animal contrast (plants make their own food from light; animals cannot and must eat) because it is the load-bearing idea that distinguishes animal nutrition and sets up food chains.

Teach food groups by FUNCTION not just name (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats for energy/warmth, vitamins & minerals for health, fibre to keep the gut working, water for everything) so grouping is meaningful.
Make 'right types AND amounts' concrete with consequences (too little calcium → weak bones; too little vitamin C → illness; too much sugar → unhealthy) rather than an abstract 'balance'.
Use real or pictured foods children eat and have them sort and build meals, connecting to their own diet.
Distinguish 'food' from 'nutrients': a single food (e.g. an egg) contains several nutrients — avoid one-food-one-group oversimplification where possible.
Link forward to digestion (how the body gets the nutrients out of food) and to food chains (why animals must eat other organisms).
keyRepresentations: A 'balanced plate' / Eatwell-style divided plate showing proportions of each food group
A plant-vs-animal contrast panel: plant with sun → 'makes its own food'; animal with mouth → 'must eat food'
A function strip pairing each food group with what it does for the body
Consequence cards linking a missing nutrient to a health effect (calcium→bones, vitamin C→scurvy)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking animals (or humans) can make their own food or 'get energy from the sun' like plants — the core misconception this topic must correct.
Believing 'more food is always better' or that one favourite food can be a whole diet, missing 'right amounts' and variety.
Assuming each food belongs to exactly one group, rather than most foods containing several nutrients.
Confusing 'healthy = expensive/special food' rather than balance across ordinary foods.
Thinking only 'unhealthy' people need to worry about nutrition, rather than everyone needing the right types and amounts.

learn.summary: Animal nutrition for 7–8 year-olds (UK DfE Y3 'Animals, including humans'). The load-bearing idea is that plants MAKE their own food using light while animals CANNOT and must EAT to get energy and nutrients. From there children group foods, match each group to what it does for the body (energy, growth/repair, warmth, health, gut function, hydration), and grasp that the body needs the RIGHT TYPES and RIGHT AMOUNTS — a balanced variety, not a single favourite or simply 'more'. Consequences of imbalance (weak bones without calcium, illness without vitamin C) make this concrete. The core proposed activity is a build-a-balanced-plate task with a responsive balance meter, complemented by a real classroom food-sort and a plant-vs-animal contrast that also links to food chains; alternatives (reveal poster, sorting consolidation, nutritionist dialogue) are kept for their distinct purposes.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate with a live balance meter
feedback: If the plate is piled with only sweets or cakes: 'Lots of energy from sugar, but very little for growth or health — your body needs other groups too.' If it is piled with only one non-sugary food, name what that food gives and which groups are still missing.
If variety and proportions are good: meter settles green and the cartoon body perks up — 'Right types and right amounts.'

When a deficiency pop-up appears (e.g. too little calcium over time → weak bones), explain that calcium is a mineral (in the vitamins & minerals group) found in foods such as milk, cheese and yoghurt, and let the child add one of those foods.
If two equal-sized plates score differently, draw attention to WHY: 'Same amount of food, but one has a healthy variety.'
activities.rationale: The objective is grouping foods and balancing amounts, which is a sortable, buildable task. A live balance meter is intended to make 'right types AND amounts' something the child notices through the recompute rather than a stated rule. The parallel real-food sort connects to the child's own diet as recommended in best practice.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory requirement: 'identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat'.
Main food groups and their roles for KS2 (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats, vitamins and minerals for health, fibre, water); a balanced diet uses the right amounts from each.
learnerActions: Drag on-screen food cards onto a plate while a health/balance meter responds to what you add (in the classroom, do a parallel hands-on sort using real packets and pictures of your own meals).
Pile the plate with only cakes and sweets and read the meter: it swings to 'too much sugar — not enough for growth', with a cartoon body looking sluggish.
Now swap in some protein, vegetables, a carbohydrate and water; watch the meter settle into the green as the body perks up.
Compare two plates with the SAME total amount of food but different variety, and say which scores healthier and why.
When a nutrient is missing, read the consequence pop-up (e.g. too little calcium over a long time → weak bones; too little vitamin C over a long time → illness) and add a food that fixes it.
activities.intendedInsight: It is the right TYPES and AMOUNTS together — a balanced variety — that keep the body healthy, not quantity alone; the same total food scores differently depending on its variety.

activities.title: Plant makes food vs animal must eat
feedback: If the child says the dog can feed on sunlight: contrast directly — plants make their own food using light; animals cannot do this and must eat.
Correct answer: the dog cannot make food; it must eat, and its energy comes from the food it eats.
On the food chain: both the cow and the lion get their energy from food (grass, then the cow); the energy in bread began in a plant that captured sunlight.
Clarify a common slip: plants DO get nutrition — they just make their own rather than eating it, so saying 'plants get no nutrition' is wrong.
activities.rationale: This heterotroph/autotroph contrast is the core misconception to correct and the idea that sets up food chains. A responsive toggle is intended to make the 'make vs eat' distinction observable, and the food-chain question links the energy animals eat back to plants.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory requirement: 'identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat'.
NGSS frames the idea that food provides animals with the materials and energy they need within 5-PS3-1 / LS1.C, rather than a food-groups PE.
learnerActions: Watch or act out two side-by-side cases: a plant in sunlight whose food bar fills on its own, and an animal whose hunger bar only refills when you feed it.
Toggle sunlight on and off: the plant's food bar fills only when light is on, while the animal's hunger bar does not respond to sunlight at all.
Feed the animal a meal and watch its hunger bar refill, then say in your own words why the animal needed the food.
Answer: 'Can a dog just sit in the sun and make its own food like a sunflower?' and explain where the dog's energy actually comes from.
Trace a food chain: a cow eats grass and a lion eats the cow — say how each gets its energy, and where the energy in a slice of bread first came from (the plant, which captured it from the sun).
activities.intendedInsight: Animals cannot make their own food and must eat (plants or other animals) to get energy and nutrients; plants make their own food using light, and in food chains like these the energy animals eat traces back to plants.

activities.title: Reveal-the-job food-group poster (scaffold)
feedback: When a section is revealed, restate the function in child terms and ask for one more food in that group.
On the myth-buster flap: reinforce that animals must eat; plants make their own food using light, but animals cannot.
If a child assigns a food to exactly one group, note that many foods (e.g. an egg) contain several nutrients.
activities.rationale: A reveal poster names groups and their functions and includes the plant-vs-animal myth-buster. It is a naming/revealing scaffold: it does not itself let the child actively balance amounts or experience the consequence of imbalance, so it supports but does not replace the build-a-plate task.
sourceClaims: Main food groups and their roles for KS2 (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats, vitamins and minerals for health, fibre, water); a balanced diet uses the right amounts from each.
learnerActions: Tap or lift each section of a balanced-plate / food-group poster to reveal the group name and its job (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats for energy/warmth, vitamins & minerals for health, fibre for the gut, water for everything).
Open a myth-buster flap: 'Can animals make their own food like plants?' and read the answer.
Name a food you ate recently and say which group(s) it belongs to.
activities.intendedInsight: Each food group has a job in the body, and grouping foods is meaningful when tied to function.

activities.title: Sort-and-match consolidation
feedback: For a mis-sort, point back to the food's main nutrient and the group's job.
For 'why can't a cat make its own food?': reinforce that animals must eat; plants make food using light, but animals cannot.
If the child accepts 'humans make food from sunlight', re-run the plant-vs-animal contrast.
activities.rationale: Sorting, matching and single-answer questions check the objectives and rehearse the reasoning. On their own they do not build the quantitative balancing intuition, so they follow the active build task rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Main food groups and their roles for KS2 (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats, vitamins and minerals for health, fibre, water); a balanced diet uses the right amounts from each.
learnerActions: Sort a set of food cards into groups by their main nutrient (carbohydrate / protein / fat / vitamins & minerals / fibre / water), noting foods such as eggs that could go in more than one group.
Match each group to its function.
Answer 'why can't a cat make its own food?' and explain in a sentence.
Spot and reject a wrong claim such as 'humans make food from sunlight'.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate naming food groups, linking them to function, and the reason animals cannot make their own food.

activities.title: Ask-a-nutritionist curiosity dialogue
feedback: For 'only chips': name what is missing (growth, health) and what too much of one thing does.
For 'is more always better?': emphasise right amounts, not just quantity.
For 'why can't I make my own food?': animals must eat; plants make their own food using light, but animals cannot.
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue can motivate the balance idea through the child's own curiosity. It is a motivational complement; for the core sorting/balancing objective, actively building a plate may be a more direct route.
learnerActions: Ask a nutritionist/'body' character questions such as 'What happens if I only eat chips?', 'Is more food always better?' and 'Why can't I make my own food?'.
Predict the answer before revealing it, then compare.
Use the answer to plan one change to a one-sided plate.
activities.intendedInsight: A one-sided or over-large diet causes problems; the body needs variety and the right amounts, and animals must eat to get nutrients.

constraints: Keep at the level of grouping foods and matching each group to its job; detailed nutrient chemistry is KS3 and out of scope.
The reveal poster is a naming/revealing scaffold: it does not let a child actively balance amounts or experience the consequence of imbalance, so pair it with the active build task.
Sort/match/single-answer questions consolidate and check recall and reasoning but do not by themselves build the quantitative balancing intuition.
Avoid one-food-one-group oversimplification: note that most foods (e.g. an egg) contain several nutrients.
Keep 'right types AND amounts' concrete via consequences (calcium→bones, vitamin C→illness, too much sugar→unhealthy) rather than an abstract 'balance'.
Use real or pictured foods the children actually eat so grouping connects to their own diet; keep the physical sort distinct from the on-screen responsive meter.
A balance meter is an illustrative teaching device, not a clinical nutrition assessment; thresholds are simplified for learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The British Nutrition Foundation / Eatwell claim is marked verified:false in the source row; treat food-group role statements as standard KS2 guidance pending check.
Self-audit: 'plants get no nutrition' is a listed misconception — guidance clarifies plants DO get nutrition by making their own food, so no learner-facing action asserts plants are nutrition-free.
Self-audit: the balance-meter thresholds and 'green/sluggish' outcomes are pedagogical simplifications, not measured nutritional facts; framed as a teaching device in constraints.
The source assessment's probeDeeper food-chain and energy-origin questions have been incorporated into the plant-vs-animal activity to preserve the forward link to food chains.

The original 3D 'poor-fit' entry asserted a 3D scene 'adds cost without insight'; this reflects an internal catalog ranking rather than an established pedagogical law and was dropped rather than propagated as a universal claim.

probeDeeper: Where did the energy in a slice of bread originally come from?
Name some different food groups — does it matter if you only ever ate one of them?
A cow eats grass and a lion eats the cow. Do both get their energy from food? How?
Why can't you live on sunlight and water the way a sunflower does?
assess.correctAnswer: No — animals like the dog cannot make their own food; they must EAT food (plants or other animals) to get energy and nutrients. Only plants can make their own food using sunlight. The dog's energy comes from the food it eats, which is why animals must find and eat food to survive.

errorPatterns.pattern: animals can make their own food like plants (e.g. from sunlight)
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast plants (make their own food using light) with animals (must eat); only plants photosynthesise
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — sitting in the sun gives the dog energy just like a plant
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the dog can make food by sitting in the sun

errorPatterns.pattern: food just fills you up; it doesn't give energy
errorPatterns.nextMove: link food to energy — animals get all their energy from what they eat
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies that food is the energy source

errorPatterns.pattern: all foods are the same, or one food provides everything
errorPatterns.nextMove: introduce the main food groups and that the body needs a range of them
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe cannot name different food groups or their roles

errorPatterns.pattern: plants don't need nutrition because they don't 'eat'
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify plants DO get nutrition — they just make their own food rather than eating it

responseLevels.gap: Says animals can make their own food, or that food gives no energy; cannot name food groups.
responseLevels.full: Explains that animals cannot make their own food and must eat to get energy and nutrients (unlike plants), names the main food groups, and describes consequences of too much or too little of one.
responseLevels.partial: Names food groups and knows animals eat, but as separate facts — cannot clearly contrast animals (must eat) with plants (make their own food), or link food to energy and the effect of imbalance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A plant can sit in the sunshine and make its own food. Can a dog do the same — just sit in the sun and make its own food? Explain why or why not, and where a dog's energy actually comes from.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks animals can make food like plants, or that sunlight feeds animals, answers 'yes'; a child who knows animals must eat while plants make their own food says no and locates the dog's energy in its food. The reason tier is decisive.
